metadata.name: Signals and Systems Multilingual Retrieval Evaluation Set
metadata.notes: Curated benchmark for cross-lingual and code-mixed retrieval evaluation in engineering domain. Academic corpus chunks are English-medium; queries span English, Telugu script, Romanized Telugu, and code-mixed Telugu-English.

corpus.text: Convolution is a fundamental mathematical operation used to determine the output of a continuous or discrete Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) system. For continuous-time systems, the output y(t) is given by the convolution integral of the input signal x(t) and the system impulse response h(t): y(t) = integral_{-inf}^{inf} x(tau) h(t - tau) dtau. Convolution satisfies commutative, associative, and distributive properties.

A Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) system satisfies two core properties: linearity (superposition and homogeneity) and time-invariance. A system is linear if the response to a weighted sum of inputs equals the weighted sum of individual outputs. It is time-invariant if a time shift in the input signal produces an identical time shift in the output response. An LTI system is completely characterized by its unit impulse response h(t).

The Continuous-Time Fourier Transform (CTFT) represents a continuous-time signal in the frequency domain. The Fourier transform X(omega) of a signal x(t) is defined by X(omega) = integral_{-inf}^{inf} x(t) e^{-j omega t} dt. It decomposes a signal into its constituent complex sinusoidal frequency components, providing the magnitude spectrum and phase spectrum of the signal.

Key properties of the Fourier Transform include linearity, time shifting, frequency shifting, differentiation in time, integration, and duality. The convolution property states that convolution in the time domain corresponds to point-wise multiplication in the frequency domain: F{x(t) * h(t)} = X(omega) H(omega). This property simplifies system analysis enormously.

The Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem establishes the condition under which a continuous-time bandlimited signal can be completely reconstructed from its discrete samples. If a signal x(t) has a highest frequency component of B Hz (or omega_m rad/s), the sampling frequency f_s must be strictly greater than twice the maximum frequency: f_s >= 2 * B. The minimum sampling rate 2 * B is termed the Nyquist rate.

When a signal is sampled at a frequency lower than the Nyquist rate (f_s < 2*B), high frequency spectral components fold over into the lower frequency range. This distortion phenomenon is called aliasing. To prevent aliasing, an anti-aliasing low-pass filter must be applied before sampling to attenuate frequencies exceeding f_s / 2. An ideal low-pass interpolation filter reconstructs the continuous signal.

corpus.section: Laplace Transform and Region of Convergence
corpus.text: The bilateral Laplace Transform generalizes the Fourier transform to complex frequency s = sigma + j omega: X(s) = integral_{-inf}^{inf} x(t) e^{-st} dt. The Region of Convergence (ROC) is the set of values of s in the complex plane for which the integral converges. The ROC cannot contain any poles, is bounded by vertical lines, and determines system stability and causality.

corpus.section: System Stability and Poles in Laplace Domain
corpus.text: For a continuous-time LTI system with transfer function H(s), the system is Bounded-Input Bounded-Output (BIBO) stable if and only if the Region of Convergence (ROC) includes the j omega imaginary axis. For a causal system, stability requires that all poles of H(s) strictly lie in the open left-half of the complex s-plane (Re(s) < 0).

The Z-transform is the discrete-time counterpart of the Laplace transform, mapping discrete-time sequences x[n] into the complex z-plane: X(z) = sum_{n=-inf}^{inf} x[n] z^{-n}. The ROC is a ring centered at the origin of the z-plane. A discrete-time LTI system is BIBO stable if and only if the ROC of its transfer function H(z) contains the unit circle |z| = 1.

Signals are categorized based on their total energy E and average power P. An energy signal has finite total energy (0 < E < infinity) and zero average power (P = 0). A power signal has infinite total energy (E = infinity) and finite, non-zero average power (0 < P < infinity). Periodic signals and random processes are typically power signals, whereas transient pulses are energy signals.
